claim: A dedicated Russian practical transcription of Burmese geographical names was published by V. G. Epstein in 1959.
A 1978 institutional instruction for Russian transmission of Burmese geographical names is also documented, showing continuity beyond the 1959 Epstein rules.
A 1958 Epstein item concerning transcription of Burmese proper names is retained as a historical bibliographic lead; its article-level record was not independently verified in the present review.
The Russian practical tradition distinguishes onset and final behaviour and contains explicit medial, vowel/rime and final rules.
Russian practical transcription does not encode Burmese tone in the ordinary Cyrillic output.
The current Ukrainian state orthography standard provides the normative target-language basis for practical transcription; the 2026 standard entered into force on 2026-03-28.
Serbian foreign-name transcription scholarship treats pronunciation, established usage, target-language naturalness, simplicity and consistency as relevant adaptation criteria.
No dedicated Burmese-specific Bulgarian practical transcription rule set was established in the present review.

Mooney and Repetti-Ludlow (2021) argue that the Burmese vowel alternations they analyze are tone-independent and can be derived from sonority-sequencing preferences; the project therefore does not encode a direct tone-to-vowel rule from this source alone.
scope: Central Burmese vowel alternations in the environments analyzed by the study

claim: Myanmar virama U+1039 functions as a stacker in consonant-conjunct structure; a virama not followed by a consonant in the parsed conjunct is malformed orthography and must not be silently discarded.
scope: Modern Burmese syllable structure and U+1039 virama/conjunct parsing

scope: Hugging Face dataset card and snapshot metadata

claim: The Burmese Wiktionary dataset card declares CC BY 4.0.
Myanmar Wiktionary local policy states CC BY-SA 3.0 Unported and GNU Free Documentation License (GFDL).

myG2P Version 2.0 publishes a five-field Burmese pronunciation dictionary with orthography, syllable segmentation, romanized pronunciation and IPA; its README states that the dictionary is based mainly on Myanmar Language Commission dictionary words and is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
OpenSLR SLR80 lists a CC BY-SA 4.0 license for manually quality-checked volunteer Burmese sentence recordings and orthographic transcripts; the resource does not provide IPA labels.
Unicode identifies four modern Burmese medial slots as modified forms of ya, ra, wa and ha; this is orthographic evidence, not invariant IPA mapping.
Ishida 2026 describes U+103B and U+103C as normally /j/ and as producing palatalized outcomes after velar stops; descriptive candidate, not complete acoustic rule table.
scope: Modern printed Burmese; medial ya/ra and preceding onset class

claim: Ishida describes U+103D as /w/ but notes that it may also represent /ʊ/ in specific vowel/rime environments.
scope: Modern printed Burmese; medial wa and vowel/rime context

claim: Ishida describes U+103E as an aspiration marker and documents selected /ʃ/ outcomes, rather than a universal independent /h/ segment.
scope: Modern printed Burmese; medial ha and specific onset combinations

claim: Thu et al. (2016) use 25,000 training words, three 100-word open test sets and a separate 100-word closed set drawn from training; closed-set scores are not independent holdout evidence.
Oo et al. (2020) describe SLR80 as 2,528 utterances from 20 female speakers recorded in Yangon; paper does not specify a regional dialect for speakers.
Oo et al. (2020) describe a Thrax WFST Burmese G2P grammar producing IPA; paper gives a GitHub URL but does not identify a specific grammar license.
scope: §4.4 and references; PDF pp.6-7 and p.9

claim: Yanson (2015) argues that modern Burmese sound changes may not be reflected in standard dictionary/textbook pronunciations; full text unavailable, so no runtime rule is derived.

Green (2002) models Burmese syllables as C(G)V((V)C) and gives /mj/ onset examples mjè: 'earth' and mjɛʔ 'eye'; this supports a glide-bearing onset analysis but does not map a Unicode medial sign by itself.

Green (2002) analyzes coda /N/ as placeless and says it is realized through nasalization of the preceding vowel, with approximate coronal articulation after monophthongs and approximate velar articulation after diphthongs.
scope: §1.2, pp.4-5; coda inventory and place realization

claim: Green (2002) describes four tones in major syllables but only low, high and creaky tones in nasal rhymes; checked tone is excluded from nasal rhymes.

Pinned Google Thrax grammar maps U+103B/U+103C to medial tokens -y/-r, U+103D/U+103E to -w/-h, reorders -h before other medials, maps -y and -r to /j/ and -w to /w/, and applies onset/rime-specific alternatives and weights.
scope: my/burmese.grm: UTF8_TO_GRAPHEME, reorder_medials, g2p_initial, g2p_medial and g2p_nucleus; pinned commit a90601024f07ab7e96c911243324e0adeb16da96
